title: BREE 216: Bioresource Engineering Materials
course_note: A teaching catalogue. The supplier entities are fictional and no order can be placed; the prices are anchored to published August 2026 supplier and commodity data and are then perturbed per variant. Version 3 adds cradle-to-gate carbon, water, a realistic end-of-life recovery kept apart from the property-sheet recyclability, the lowest useful service temperature, and, for a process, energy and carbon per unit of process. Version 4 adds the challenge requirements on each brief. Version 6 replaces the em dashes in the prose with colons. Prices and figures are unchanged.

suppliers.name: Laurentian Metal Supply
suppliers.shipping: Next-day GTA/Montréal · 2–4 day rest of QC/ON
suppliers.blurb: Service centre stocking hot-rolled, cold-drawn, alloy and abrasion-resistant steels plus 6000-series aluminium. Everything is cut to size and priced by mass, so you can compare grades on a true $/kg basis.
suppliers.policy: Prices are per kilogram of finished cut mass unless noted. Saw-cut charge applies to every cut piece. Mill test reports available on request (see Macdonald Fab Works, MFW-CERT-CMTR).
suppliers.minimum_order_note: 25 kg minimum on plate; 1 length minimum on structural sections.

suppliers.name: Boréal Stainless & Alloy
suppliers.shipping: 2–3 day QC/ON · sanitary items ship in sealed bags
suppliers.blurb: Corrosion-resistant alloys for food, dairy and chemical service. Sanitary tube and fittings carry 3-A / FDA documentation; every heat is traceable to a mill certificate.
suppliers.policy: 316L carries a nickel-and-molybdenum surcharge that moves weekly: quotes are firm for 14 days only. Surface finish is priced separately from base metal.
suppliers.minimum_order_note: 10 kg minimum on sheet and plate; single-piece minimum on fittings.

suppliers.name: Cascades Polymer & Pipe Co.
suppliers.shipping: Coils and sheets ship LTL freight · straight lengths max 6 m
suppliers.blurb: Pipe, sheet and glazing in the full commodity-polymer range. Straight lengths are sold by the metre and cut to order; anything under 3 m carries a cutting fee, exactly as in the trade.
suppliers.policy: Pipe is priced per metre of nominal size. Cutting fee applies to lengths under 3 m. Polymer pressure ratings are stated at 23 °C: de-rate for service temperature using the chart on each product page.
suppliers.minimum_order_note: 3 m minimum on pipe; full-sheet minimum on rigid sheet stock.

suppliers.name: Terrafibre Composites
suppliers.shipping: Fabric on rolls · resin is regulated dangerous goods (ground only)
suppliers.blurb: Reinforcement fabrics from E-glass to Québec-grown flax and hemp, matched with petroleum and bio-based resin systems. Fibre-volume-fraction calculators on every fabric page.
suppliers.policy: Fabric is priced per square metre of as-woven area. Finished laminate cost must include resin uptake: use the resin-ratio calculator, do not quote fabric price alone.
suppliers.minimum_order_note: 2 m² minimum on fabric; 4 L minimum on resin systems.

suppliers.name: Vulcan Hard Materials
suppliers.shipping: Blanks 3–5 days · coating services 7–10 working days
suppliers.blurb: Wear-critical materials and the surface engineering to go with them. If your component is failing by abrasion, erosion or edge rounding, the answer is on this page.
suppliers.policy: Carbide is priced by finished mass: density is 14.5–15.0 g/cm³, roughly twice steel, so a carbide part costs far more than the $/kg figure alone suggests. Coating services are priced per square decimetre of coated surface.
suppliers.minimum_order_note: Single-piece minimum on blanks; 5 dm² minimum on coating services.

suppliers.name: Macdonald Fab Works
suppliers.shipping: Customer-supplied material accepted · drop-off or courier
suppliers.blurb: The process side of the cost equation. A material is only as cheap as it is to make into a part: price your fabrication route here before you defend a material choice.
suppliers.policy: Shop time is billed in 0.25 h increments with a 1 h minimum. Heat treatment and galvanizing are priced per kilogram of load. Tooling is a one-time non-recurring charge that must be amortised over your production volume.
suppliers.minimum_order_note: 1 hour minimum on all shop time; 25 kg minimum load on heat treatment.

lines.name: ASTM A36 / CSA 44W hot-rolled plate
lines.description: The default structural mild steel. Cheap, tough, weldable with any process, and available everywhere: which is exactly why it is the baseline every alternative must beat.
lines.fabrication: Oxy-fuel or plasma cut, press-brake formed, GMAW welded. Must be painted or galvanised for outdoor service.
lines.end_of_life: Ferrous scrap is magnetically separated and re-melted in an electric arc furnace with no loss of quality. Steel is the most recycled material on earth by mass.

lines.name: ASTM A36 / CSA 44W hot-rolled plate
lines.description: Heavier gauge A36 for base plates, hopper walls and bolted connections. Price per kilogram drops slightly with thickness because rolling cost is spread over more mass.
lines.fabrication: Plasma or waterjet cut, GMAW/SMAW welded, hot-dip galvanised for outdoor structures.
lines.end_of_life: Ferrous scrap is magnetically separated and re-melted in an electric arc furnace with no loss of quality. Steel is the most recycled material on earth by mass.

lines.name: ASTM A36 / CSA 44W hot-rolled plate
lines.description: Heavy plate for machine frames, digester foundations and bearing blocks. Note the through-thickness properties are not guaranteed: specify Z-quality if you are loading it in the short-transverse direction.
lines.fabrication: Waterjet or plasma cut, multi-pass welding with preheat above 20 mm.
lines.end_of_life: Ferrous scrap is magnetically separated and re-melted in an electric arc furnace with no loss of quality. Steel is the most recycled material on earth by mass.

lines.name: AISI 1018 cold-drawn round bar
lines.description: Low-carbon bar with a bright cold-drawn finish, good dimensional tolerance and excellent machinability. Case-harden it if you need a wear surface on a tough core.
lines.fabrication: Turned and milled as supplied; carburise (MFW-HT-CASE) for a hard case over a ductile core.
lines.end_of_life: Ferrous scrap is magnetically separated and re-melted in an electric arc furnace with no loss of quality. Steel is the most recycled material on earth by mass.

lines.name: AISI 1045 medium-carbon round bar
lines.description: The workhorse shafting steel, supplied hot-rolled at about 163 HB. Quench-and-temper takes it to roughly 300 HB and 450 MPa yield, and it flame- or induction-hardens locally for journals and wear pads.
lines.fabrication: Turn, mill, then induction- or through-harden (MFW-HT-QT). Weldability drops sharply above 0.4 %C: preheat required.
lines.end_of_life: Ferrous scrap is magnetically separated and re-melted in an electric arc furnace with no loss of quality. Steel is the most recycled material on earth by mass.

lines.name: AISI 1080 high-carbon flat bar
lines.description: High-carbon steel that hardens to 58–62 HRC. It takes and keeps a keen edge, which is what makes it the traditional plough-share and chipper-knife material: at the cost of brittleness and poor weldability.
lines.fabrication: Profile cut soft, grind the edge, then austenitise, oil-quench and temper (MFW-HT-QT). Never weld in the hardened condition.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as alloy scrap. Hardened blades are usually replaced rather than repaired, so the replacement cycle dominates their lifetime footprint.

lines.name: AISI 4140 alloy steel round bar, annealed
lines.description: Chromium-molybdenum steel supplied soft for machining. It is the standard choice when 1045 is not strong enough and tool steel is overkill.
lines.fabrication: Rough machine annealed, quench and temper to 28–34 HRC, finish machine. Nitride (MFW-HT-NITRIDE) for a wear surface without distortion.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as low-alloy scrap; Cr and Mo are recovered in the melt.

lines.name: AISI 4140 alloy steel round bar, Q&T 28–32 HRC
lines.description: Pre-hardened 4140 saves you a heat-treatment cycle and the distortion that comes with it. Yield strength is nearly four times A36 for under three times the price per kilogram.
lines.fabrication: Machine in the hardened condition with carbide tooling. Weld only with preheat and post-weld temper.
lines.end_of_life: As annealed 4140, plus the heat-treatment energy already embodied in the supplied condition.

lines.name: AISI 5160 spring steel flat bar
lines.description: Chromium spring steel, the leaf-spring alloy, supplied hot-rolled and soft enough to cut and form. Quenched and tempered it reaches about 1450 MPa yield and 1585 MPa tensile at 45 to 50 HRC with the ability to absorb repeated impact without cracking, which is why chipper knives and cultivator shanks are made from it. Price the heat treatment (MFW-HT-QT) with the bar.
lines.fabrication: Hot-form or profile cut soft, austenitise 830 °C, oil quench, temper 400–500 °C to 45–50 HRC.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as alloy scrap. Hardened blades are usually replaced rather than repaired, so the replacement cycle dominates their lifetime footprint.

lines.name: AR400 abrasion-resistant plate
lines.description: Through-hardened quenched-and-tempered plate at 360–440 HB. Roughly three times the abrasive wear life of A36 for about twice the price: usually the cheapest way to buy wear resistance in a large area.
lines.fabrication: Plasma, laser or oxy-fuel cut; the heat-affected zone softens a few millimetres back from the edge, so finish-machine cut edges that will see wear. Weld with low-hydrogen consumables and controlled interpass temperature.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as alloy scrap. Its value case is that one AR400 wear part replaces roughly three mild-steel ones, cutting the replacement footprint threefold.

lines.name: AR500 abrasion-resistant plate
lines.description: Harder grade for severe sliding abrasion: chute liners, hopper throats, pellet-mill wear rings. The extra 100 HB buys wear life but costs you toughness and formability.
lines.fabrication: Plasma, laser or waterjet cut; waterjet leaves no softened zone. Bend radii must be at least 4× thickness. Weld with strict preheat.
lines.end_of_life: As AR400; the harder grade buys further wear life at a small additional production carbon cost.

lines.name: Hardox 450 equivalent wear plate
lines.description: Premium wear plate with guaranteed impact toughness at −40 °C: the distinguishing feature versus generic AR400/AR500. Worth the premium when the part is both abraded and impacted, as in a chipper anvil.
lines.fabrication: Laser cut, cold formable to 3× thickness, weldable without preheat under 10 mm.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as alloy scrap; guaranteed −40 °C toughness avoids the brittle-fracture replacement that drives waste in cold service.

lines.name: G90 hot-dip galvanised sheet, ASTM A653
lines.description: Mild steel with a 275 g/m² zinc coating on both faces: roughly 20 µm per side. In rural atmosphere the zinc gives 40+ years of sacrificial protection; in a fertiliser hopper it is consumed in a season.
lines.fabrication: Shear or laser cut, roll-form or brake. Every cut edge exposes bare steel: zinc-rich paint the edges or accept sacrificial edge creep.
lines.end_of_life: Zinc volatilises in the electric arc furnace and is recovered from the flue dust; the steel itself recycles normally. Galvanising adds roughly 0.2 kg CO2/kg but removes decades of repainting.

lines.name: Galvanised HSS square tube, ASTM A500B
lines.description: The greenhouse and equipment-frame standard. Closed section gives high torsional stiffness for its mass, and the hot-dip galvanising survives humid growing environments far better than painted steel.
lines.fabrication: Cold-saw cut, GMAW weld (grind galvanising back 25 mm from the joint and re-coat), or bolt with self-drilling fasteners to avoid burning the zinc.
lines.end_of_life: Zinc volatilises in the electric arc furnace and is recovered from the flue dust; the steel itself recycles normally. Galvanising adds roughly 0.2 kg CO2/kg but removes decades of repainting.

lines.name: Galvanised HSS square tube, ASTM A500B
lines.description: Heavier wall for columns and highly loaded rafters. Going from 3.2 to 4.8 mm wall raises mass about 30 % and second moment of area about 35 %, so the heavier wall buys stiffness only in proportion to its mass: a bigger, thinner tube is usually the more efficient answer.
lines.fabrication: Same as 3.2 mm wall; the heavier section is more forgiving of weld heat input.
lines.end_of_life: Zinc volatilises in the electric arc furnace and is recovered from the flue dust; the steel itself recycles normally. Galvanising adds roughly 0.2 kg CO2/kg but removes decades of repainting.

lines.name: Galvanised HSS square tube, ASTM A500B
lines.description: Main-column section for wide-span greenhouse and silo structures. Section modulus is roughly three times the 50 × 4.8 tube for about 2.2 times the mass, a good illustration of why depth beats mass in bending.
lines.fabrication: Cold-saw cut, welded base-plate connections, hot-dip re-galvanise the assembly (MFW-GALV-HD).
lines.end_of_life: Zinc volatilises in the electric arc furnace and is recovered from the flue dust; the steel itself recycles normally. Galvanising adds roughly 0.2 kg CO2/kg but removes decades of repainting.

lines.name: Galvanised steel pipe, Schedule 40
lines.description: Round galvanised pipe: the traditional hoop-house arch. Round sections shed snow and wind loads well and can be roll-bent to a radius, which square tube resists.
lines.fabrication: Roll-bend cold, swage or slip-fit joints, or weld with zinc removed and re-coated.
lines.end_of_life: Zinc volatilises in the electric arc furnace and is recovered from the flue dust; the steel itself recycles normally. Galvanising adds roughly 0.2 kg CO2/kg but removes decades of repainting.

lines.name: 6061-T6 aluminium plate
lines.description: The general-purpose structural aluminium. Specific strength is roughly triple A36, it forms a self-healing oxide film, and it needs no coating outdoors: but it costs about twice as much per kilogram and only a third the stiffness.
lines.fabrication: Router or waterjet cut, GMAW/GTAW weld with 4043 or 5356 filler. Note that welding anneals the T6 temper in the heat-affected zone, dropping local strength by about 40 %.
lines.end_of_life: Re-melting takes about 5 % of primary energy, but alloy families must be kept separate: mixed extrusion and sheet scrap downgrades to cast alloy and never returns to structural use.

lines.name: 6061-T6 aluminium round bar
lines.description: Free-machining structural bar. Cuts three to four times faster than steel, which often makes the finished-part cost lower than steel despite the higher material price.
lines.fabrication: Turn and mill at high surface speed with polished-flute tooling; anodise for extra surface hardness.
lines.end_of_life: Re-melting takes about 5 % of primary energy, but alloy families must be kept separate: mixed extrusion and sheet scrap downgrades to cast alloy and never returns to structural use.

lines.name: 6063-T5 extruded angle
lines.description: Architectural extrusion alloy: lower strength than 6061 but far better extrudability, so complex glazing-bar and channel profiles are economical. This is what most greenhouse glazing frames are made from.
lines.fabrication: Mitre cut, bolt or rivet assembly. Custom die profiles are available (MFW-EXTRUDE-DIE): worth it above roughly 300 m of production.
lines.end_of_life: Re-melting takes about 5 % of primary energy, but alloy families must be kept separate: mixed extrusion and sheet scrap downgrades to cast alloy and never returns to structural use.

lines.name: 6061-T6 square tube
lines.description: Direct like-for-like alternative to the galvanised steel HSS above: same outside dimensions, one third the mass per metre, no coating needed: and a little more expensive per metre. Compare the two on the compare tool.
lines.fabrication: Mitre cut, GMAW weld or use bolted corner castings for demountable frames.
lines.end_of_life: Re-melting takes about 5 % of primary energy, but alloy families must be kept separate: mixed extrusion and sheet scrap downgrades to cast alloy and never returns to structural use.

lines.name: 5052-H32 marine-grade aluminium sheet
lines.description: Magnesium-alloyed sheet with the best corrosion resistance of the common aluminiums, including resistance to salt and fertiliser splash. It also forms far better than 6061, so it is the sheet-metal choice for hopper and tank skins.
lines.fabrication: Shear or laser cut, press-brake to tight radii, GTAW weld with 5356 filler.
lines.end_of_life: Re-melting takes about 5 % of primary energy, but alloy families must be kept separate: mixed extrusion and sheet scrap downgrades to cast alloy and never returns to structural use.

lines.name: 7075-T651 aluminium plate
lines.description: Zinc-alloyed aluminium with steel-level yield strength at a third the density. It is also essentially unweldable, susceptible to stress-corrosion cracking, and double the price of 6061: specify it only when specific strength genuinely governs.
lines.fabrication: Machined from solid and mechanically fastened. Anodise or alclad for corrosion protection.
lines.end_of_life: High zinc and copper content makes 7075 scrap hard to place; most of it is downcycled into cast alloy.

lines.name: Grey cast iron bar, class 30
lines.description: Graphite flakes make grey iron self-lubricating and give it exceptional vibration damping: roughly ten times mild steel. It has essentially no ductility, so never use it where an impact or tensile overload is credible.
lines.fabrication: Machined from continuous-cast bar or sand cast to shape. Not weldable by conventional means.
lines.end_of_life: Foundry returns and scrap iron are re-melted directly; cast iron has among the shortest recycling loops of any engineering material.

lines.name: Ductile iron bar, ASTM A536 65-45-12
lines.description: Spheroidal graphite gives iron real ductility: 12 % elongation versus zero for grey iron: while keeping castability and machinability. This is what modern tractor wheel hubs and gearbox housings are made of.
lines.fabrication: Sand or shell cast near net shape, then machined. Austemper (ADI) for a further doubling of strength.
lines.end_of_life: Re-melted as iron scrap; the magnesium treatment is re-applied in the new melt.

lines.name: Deformed reinforcing bar, CSA G30.18 400W
lines.description: The cheapest structural steel you can buy per kilogram: under a third the price of plate, because the surface finish and dimensional tolerance are irrelevant inside concrete. A useful lower bound for any $/kg comparison.
lines.fabrication: Shear cut and bent cold on a rebar bender; lap-spliced as a rule, and welded only to a qualified procedure because this is the W grade.
lines.end_of_life: Already made almost entirely from scrap in an electric arc furnace: the lowest-carbon steel in this catalogue, at roughly a third the footprint of plate.

lines.name: Weathering steel plate, ASTM A588 / COR-TEN A
lines.description: Copper- and chromium-bearing steel that forms a tight adherent rust layer which then stops further corrosion. It needs alternating wet and dry cycles to work: do not bury it, immerse it, or use it where runoff will stain concrete.
lines.fabrication: Cut and weld as for A36 but with matching weathering-grade consumables, otherwise the weld corrodes preferentially.
lines.end_of_life: Recycles as ordinary steel. Needs no paint over its life, which removes a recurring coating burden from the use phase.

lines.name: AISI 304 stainless sheet, 2B mill finish
lines.description: The default food-contact stainless: 18 % chromium, 8 % nickel, fully austenitic and non-magnetic. It resists most organic acids and cleaning chemicals but is attacked by chlorides: which is why dairy sanitisers push designers to 316.
lines.fabrication: Laser or waterjet cut, press-brake formed, GTAW welded with 308L filler, then passivated (MFW-PASSIVATE).
lines.end_of_life: Stainless scrap is valuable and is recycled back into stainless; typical new stainless already contains 60–70 % recycled feed.

lines.name: AISI 304L stainless plate, low carbon
lines.description: The L means carbon below 0.03 %, which prevents chromium-carbide precipitation at grain boundaries during welding. Without it a welded 304 part corrodes in a band either side of every weld: the classic weld-decay failure.
lines.fabrication: Same fabrication as 304, but no post-weld solution anneal is required, which is why every welded vessel uses the L grade.
lines.end_of_life: Stainless scrap is valuable and is recycled back into stainless; typical new stainless already contains 60–70 % recycled feed.

lines.name: AISI 316 stainless sheet, 2B mill finish
lines.description: Two to three percent molybdenum is the entire difference from 304, and it roughly triples resistance to chloride pitting. That is worth about 38 % more money: the single most common material-selection trade-off in food equipment.
lines.fabrication: Identical to 304 but weld with 316L filler. Never mix 304 and 316 in the same wetted circuit without checking galvanic compatibility.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as high-value molybdenum-bearing scrap. The 2–3 % Mo that buys chloride resistance is also what raises the carbon footprint 20 % over 304.

lines.name: AISI 316L stainless sheet, 2B mill finish
lines.description: The workhorse of dairy, brewing and pharmaceutical equipment: chloride-resistant and immune to weld sensitisation. If you are specifying a milk-contact surface and cannot justify anything else, this is the safe answer.
lines.fabrication: Laser cut, formed, GTAW or orbital welded (MFW-ORBITAL-W), passivated and documented for 3-A compliance.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as high-value molybdenum-bearing scrap. The 2–3 % Mo that buys chloride resistance is also what raises the carbon footprint 20 % over 304.

lines.name: AISI 316L sheet, No.4 brushed finish Ra ≤ 0.8 µm
lines.description: Same alloy as the sheet above with a directional brushed finish. The 3-A sanitary standard requires product-contact surfaces at Ra ≤ 0.8 µm; rougher surfaces harbour biofilm in the grinding grooves and cannot be reliably cleaned in place.
lines.fabrication: Handle with protective film on. Always orient the brush lines to drain, so cleaning solution runs along the grain rather than across it.
lines.end_of_life: As 316L; mechanical polishing adds abrasive consumption and a small energy increment.

lines.name: AISI 316L sheet, electropolished Ra ≤ 0.4 µm
lines.description: Electropolishing removes the deformed surface layer and leaves a chromium-enriched passive film. It roughly doubles pitting resistance and halves protein adhesion: but it costs 63 % more than plain 2B, so reserve it for genuinely aseptic surfaces.
lines.fabrication: Fabricate and weld first, electropolish last (MFW-ELECTROPOL). Welds must be fully penetrated and ground flush or the process will etch the crevice.
lines.end_of_life: As 316L, plus an electrolyte bath that must be treated as metal-bearing hazardous waste. The cleanest surface is the dirtiest process on this page.

lines.name: 316L sanitary tube, 3-A certified
lines.description: Seamless-quality welded tube with the internal weld bead rolled flush and polished to Ra ≤ 0.8 µm. Ordinary industrial pipe has a proud internal bead that is a guaranteed bacterial harbour: never substitute it in a milk line.
lines.fabrication: Cut with a tube saw (never an abrasive wheel: embedded grit causes pitting), deburr, orbital weld with full argon purge inside and out.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as high-value molybdenum-bearing scrap. The 2–3 % Mo that buys chloride resistance is also what raises the carbon footprint 20 % over 304.

lines.name: 304 welded tube, industrial finish
lines.description: The same geometry as the sanitary tube above at 29 % less money: because the interior is as-welded, not polished. Excellent for frames, guards and non-product-contact service; unacceptable for anything the milk touches.
lines.fabrication: Cut, deburr, GTAW weld. Use for structural and utility circuits only.
lines.end_of_life: Stainless scrap is valuable and is recycled back into stainless; typical new stainless already contains 60–70 % recycled feed.

lines.name: 316L heat-exchanger plate stock, embossed-ready
lines.description: Thin-gauge annealed strip for press-formed plate heat exchangers. The thermal conductivity of stainless is poor: 16 W/m·K against 400 for copper: so plate exchangers compensate with very thin walls and turbulent corrugations.
lines.fabrication: Deep-drawn or hydroformed into a chevron pattern, then either gasketed or vacuum-brazed into a stack.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as high-value molybdenum-bearing scrap. The 2–3 % Mo that buys chloride resistance is also what raises the carbon footprint 20 % over 304.

lines.name: 2205 duplex stainless plate
lines.description: A roughly 50/50 ferrite-austenite microstructure that doubles the yield strength of 316L while resisting chloride stress-corrosion cracking, which austenitics do not. You can often specify half the wall thickness: recovering much of the price premium.
lines.fabrication: Cut and weld with matched 2209 filler and controlled heat input; too fast a cool leaves excess ferrite and destroys toughness.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as duplex scrap. Note it carries LESS carbon than 316L despite costing more, because it substitutes nitrogen and chromium for expensive nickel.

lines.name: 904L super-austenitic plate
lines.description: High nickel, high molybdenum and a copper addition give resistance to hot sulphuric and organic acids that defeats 316L. Reserve it for digester liquor, silage effluent and similar aggressive service: it is nearly three times the price of 316L.
lines.fabrication: Weld with matching or over-alloyed filler. Requires strict cleanliness: iron contamination from carbon-steel tooling will initiate pitting.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as super-austenitic scrap; the high nickel and copper content makes it the most carbon-intensive stainless here.

lines.name: AISI 430 ferritic stainless sheet
lines.description: Chromium-only ferritic stainless with no nickel: which is why it is 30 % cheaper than 304 and why its price is far more stable. It is magnetic, less corrosion resistant and much less formable, but for dry or mildly wet service it is excellent value.
lines.fabrication: Shear and brake form with generous radii. Weldable but grain growth in the HAZ embrittles thick sections.
lines.end_of_life: Ferritic stainless contains no nickel, so its footprint is a third below 304 and its price is far more stable. Recycles readily.

lines.name: AISI 410 martensitic stainless round bar
lines.description: The only stainless family that hardens by quenching: it reaches 45 HRC and holds an edge, which is why food-processing knives and pump shafts use it. Corrosion resistance is markedly lower than 304 and drops further as hardness rises.
lines.fabrication: Machine soft, harden and temper (MFW-HT-QT), then grind and passivate. Never temper in the 400–550 °C range: it embrittles.
lines.end_of_life: Nickel-free martensitic stainless. Lower carbon than 304, but its corrosion resistance falls as hardness rises: a real trade in food service.

lines.name: 17-4 PH precipitation-hardening stainless bar
lines.description: Copper precipitates give this alloy the strength of hardened 4140 while keeping stainless-level corrosion resistance. The ageing treatment runs at only 480–620 °C, so distortion is minimal: machine to near-final size, then age.
lines.fabrication: Machine in condition A, age to H900–H1150 depending on the strength-toughness balance you need. Growth during ageing is under 0.1 %.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as specialty alloy scrap; the copper addition limits which melts will accept it.

lines.name: A4-80 (316) stainless hex bolt
lines.description: A4 is the marine grade: 316 chemistry. Use it wherever a galvanised bolt would corrode, and never mix it with plain steel in a wet joint, or the steel becomes the anode and dissolves.
lines.fabrication: Torque to a reduced value versus steel and always use an anti-seize compound: austenitic stainless galls catastrophically under thread friction.
lines.end_of_life: Fasteners recycle as stainless scrap and, unlike welds, permit disassembly: the single biggest design-for-recycling decision you can make.

lines.name: A4-70 stainless nyloc nut
lines.description: Nylon insert resists vibration loosening but caps the service temperature at 120 °C: it will not survive a hot clean-in-place cycle. Use an all-metal prevailing-torque nut on anything steam-cleaned.
lines.fabrication: Hand start, then torque. The nylon insert is good for roughly five re-uses before its locking prevailing torque falls below spec.
lines.end_of_life: Fasteners recycle as stainless scrap and, unlike welds, permit disassembly: the single biggest design-for-recycling decision you can make.

lines.name: EPDM sanitary gasket, FDA 21 CFR 177.2600
lines.description: EPDM handles hot water, steam and caustic CIP chemicals but swells badly in fats and oils. For high-fat dairy streams specify a fluoroelastomer or PTFE-envelope gasket instead: a classic elastomer-selection trap.
lines.fabrication: Install dry and centred in the clamp groove. Replace on a schedule, not on failure: a compressed-set gasket is a crevice and a contamination risk.
lines.end_of_life: Vulcanised thermoset elastomer: it cannot be re-melted. Landfill or energy recovery. Small mass, but a consumable replaced many times over the plant's life.

lines.name: Single-pin tri-clamp, 304 stainless
lines.description: Tool-free joints are what make a dairy circuit strippable for inspection. The clamp itself is not product contact, so 304 is acceptable even on a 316L line.
lines.fabrication: Hand tighten only. Over-torquing extrudes the gasket into the bore and creates the exact crevice the design is meant to eliminate.
lines.end_of_life: Recycles as 304 scrap; the tool-free joint it creates is what makes the whole circuit strippable and therefore recyclable.

lines.name: 316L GTAW filler rod
lines.description: Matched-composition filler for 316L. Filler is always chosen to match or slightly over-alloy the base metal: under-alloyed weld metal becomes the anode and corrodes preferentially in service.
lines.fabrication: Store dry. Purge the joint root with argon: unpurged stainless weld roots form a chromium-depleted sugar layer that fails in months.
lines.end_of_life: Fasteners recycle as stainless scrap and, unlike welds, permit disassembly: the single biggest design-for-recycling decision you can make.

lines.name: 2205 duplex tube
lines.description: Duplex tube for high-pressure chloride-bearing service: digester recirculation loops, brine lines, effluent handling. The higher yield strength lets you hold the same pressure with a thinner wall than 316L.
lines.fabrication: Orbital weldable with 2209 filler and strict heat-input control. Solution anneal after severe cold forming.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as duplex scrap. Note it carries LESS carbon than 316L despite costing more, because it substitutes nitrogen and chromium for expensive nickel.

lines.name: Nickel 200 sheet, commercially pure
lines.description: Commercially pure nickel is the standard for hot caustic service: sodium hydroxide CIP at concentration will attack even 316L over time. Also has four times the thermal conductivity of stainless.
lines.fabrication: GTAW weld with Ni-filler under strict cleanliness: sulphur from fingerprints or cutting fluid causes hot cracking.
lines.end_of_life: High-value nickel scrap, actively recovered. Very high production carbon: specify only where caustic service genuinely demands it.

lines.name: Titanium Grade 2 sheet, commercially pure
lines.description: Immune to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion at ambient temperature, at 56 % the density of stainless. The catch is embodied energy: roughly 590 MJ/kg, nearly ten times stainless: so life-cycle arguments cut both ways.
lines.fabrication: Must be welded in an inert chamber or with full trailing-shield argon coverage; titanium absorbs oxygen and nitrogen above 500 °C and embrittles.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled into lower-grade alloy and ferro-titanium. At roughly 38 kg CO2 per kg it is the highest-carbon metal in this catalogue: the life-cycle case must rest on a very long service life.

lines.name: PE4710 HDPE pipe, IPS SDR11
lines.description: High-density polyethylene lateral. It is fusion-welded rather than glued, which gives a joint stronger than the pipe itself: the reason HDPE dominates buried irrigation where root intrusion and joint pull-out kill PVC systems.
lines.fabrication: Butt fusion or electrofusion (CPP-HDPE-FUSE). Never solvent cement: nothing bonds to polyethylene.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: PE4710 HDPE pipe, IPS SDR11
lines.description: The standard sub-main size for field irrigation. Carbon-black loading at 2–2.5 % gives genuine long-term UV stability, unlike white PVC which chalks and embrittles in sunlight within a few seasons.
lines.fabrication: Butt-fused with a hydraulic fusion machine; the bead must be rolled back and continuous around the full circumference to pass inspection.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: PE4710 HDPE pipe, IPS SDR11
lines.description: Main-line size. Note that the price per metre rises faster than the diameter because wall thickness scales with diameter at constant SDR: doubling the bore roughly quadruples the material.
lines.fabrication: Butt fusion; requires a trench with a bedding layer of sand or screened material to prevent point loading.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: PE4710 HDPE pipe, IPS SDR11
lines.description: Trunk-main size for farm distribution or digester gas headers. At nearly 12 kg per metre it needs mechanical handling and a proper thrust-restraint design.
lines.fabrication: Butt fusion with a large-diameter machine, or flanged with a stub end and backing ring where dismantling is required.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: PE4710 HDPE coil, IPS SDR11
lines.description: Buying in coil eliminates joints: the single biggest source of leaks and the main labour cost in a drip system. Compare the effective price per metre against straight lengths plus fittings before you decide.
lines.fabrication: Uncoil in warm weather and allow it to relax before backfilling, or thermal contraction will pull the fittings apart in the first cold night.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: PVC Schedule 40 pressure pipe
lines.description: The cheapest pressure pipe on the market and easily the stiffest polymer option: over three times the modulus of HDPE. Its weaknesses are UV degradation and brittle fracture in cold weather, both fatal above ground in a Québec winter.
lines.fabrication: Solvent-cement socket joints. The joint is a chemical weld, not a glue: it needs primer, a full wet coat and a quarter-turn on assembly.
lines.end_of_life: Recyclable in principle. In practice the chlorine content contaminates mixed-plastic streams and rules out energy recovery without flue-gas scrubbing.

lines.name: PVC Schedule 40 pressure pipe
lines.description: Main-line PVC at roughly half the price of the equivalent HDPE. That saving is real, but so is the higher failure rate at joints when the ground moves: weigh installed cost, not material cost.
lines.fabrication: Solvent-cement with thrust blocks at every change of direction; PVC joints carry no tensile load.
lines.end_of_life: Recyclable in principle. In practice the chlorine content contaminates mixed-plastic streams and rules out energy recovery without flue-gas scrubbing.

lines.name: PVC Schedule 80 pressure pipe
lines.description: Thicker wall for higher pressure and the only PVC schedule that may be threaded. Note the pressure rating is quoted at 23 °C: at 50 °C you must de-rate it to about 50 % of the printed value.
lines.fabrication: Solvent weld or thread. Threading removes half the wall, so a threaded Sch 80 joint has roughly the pressure rating of plain Sch 40.
lines.end_of_life: Recyclable in principle. In practice the chlorine content contaminates mixed-plastic streams and rules out energy recovery without flue-gas scrubbing.

lines.name: CPVC Schedule 80 pipe
lines.description: Chlorinating the PVC backbone lifts the service temperature from 60 °C to 93 °C, which is what makes CPVC viable for hot cleaning circuits and solar-thermal loops. It costs roughly three times plain Sch 40.
lines.fabrication: Solvent cement with CPVC-specific one-step cement; PVC cement will not develop full strength on CPVC.
lines.end_of_life: As PVC but with additional chlorination energy and an even thinner recycling market.

lines.name: PEX-a cross-linked polyethylene tube
lines.description: Cross-linking gives polyethylene a memory and a much higher service temperature. Its real advantage in cold climates is that it expands rather than bursts on freezing: the reason it dominates in-floor heating in greenhouses.
lines.fabrication: Expansion-ring or crimp fittings. Cross-linked material cannot be fusion welded or recycled by melting, which is its main sustainability liability.
lines.end_of_life: Cross-linked and therefore not re-meltable: this is the sustainability price of its freeze tolerance. Compare it with PE-RT, which behaves similarly and still recycles.

lines.name: Polypropylene homopolymer sheet
lines.description: The lightest common engineering polymer at 0.905 g/cm³: it floats. Outstanding resistance to acids, alkalis and most fertiliser salts, which makes it the natural liner for a corrosive hopper.
lines.fabrication: Hot-gas or extrusion welded with PP rod; CNC routed. Cannot be solvent cemented: no solvent attacks it, which is precisely the point.
lines.end_of_life: Polypropylene has the lowest production carbon of the commodity polymers and is recyclable, but it embrittles near 0 °C: a real constraint in Canadian outdoor service.

lines.name: UHMW-PE sheet, virgin
lines.description: Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene has the lowest coefficient of friction of any commercial solid apart from PTFE, and it outwears carbon steel in sliding abrasion against grain and wood chips. That is why silo and hopper liners are made from it.
lines.fabrication: Routed or sawn; fastened with countersunk bolts and oversized holes to allow for its very large thermal movement: 200 µm/m·K, sixteen times steel.
lines.end_of_life: Technically re-meltable, but the very high molecular weight makes it hard to reprocess; most worn liners are landfilled.

lines.name: UHMW-PE round bar
lines.description: Bar stock for sprockets, guide rollers and dry-running bushings in wash-down environments where a greased bronze bearing would be a contamination risk.
lines.fabrication: Turn and mill with sharp positive-rake tooling and no coolant. Expect the part to grow slightly after machining as residual stress relaxes.
lines.end_of_life: Technically re-meltable, but the very high molecular weight makes it hard to reprocess; most worn liners are landfilled.

lines.name: Twin-wall polycarbonate glazing, UV-coated
lines.description: The greenhouse glazing benchmark: about 80 % light transmission, a U-value near 3.3 W/m²·K thanks to the trapped air cell, and 200 times the impact resistance of glass. The co-extruded UV layer is the only thing standing between it and yellowing: it must face outward.
lines.fabrication: Cut with a fine-tooth blade, seal the top flute with solid tape and the bottom with vented tape so condensate drains. Allow 3 mm per metre of thermal expansion in the glazing bar.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoplastic and re-meltable, but UV-degraded glazing is downcycled rather than reglazed. A 16 mm sheet lasting 25 years beats an 8 mm sheet replaced twice.

lines.name: Triple-wall polycarbonate glazing, UV-coated
lines.description: Three walls and 16 mm of depth drop the U-value to about 2.3 W/m²·K: roughly a 30 % heating-energy saving over 8 mm twin-wall, at 77 % more cost and about 6 % less light. That trade sits at the heart of any cold-climate greenhouse brief.
lines.fabrication: As for twin-wall, but the greater depth needs a wider glazing bar and heavier purlin spacing.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoplastic and re-meltable, but UV-degraded glazing is downcycled rather than reglazed. A 16 mm sheet lasting 25 years beats an 8 mm sheet replaced twice.

lines.name: Solid polycarbonate sheet, UV-coated both faces
lines.description: Optically clear, essentially unbreakable, and a poor insulator: a single skin has a U-value near 5.4 W/m²·K. Use it for end walls, doors and anywhere clarity or impact matters more than heat loss.
lines.fabrication: Cold-formable to a generous radius, routed and drilled with oversized holes. Never clean with ammonia: it crazes.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoplastic and re-meltable, but UV-degraded glazing is downcycled rather than reglazed. A 16 mm sheet lasting 25 years beats an 8 mm sheet replaced twice.

lines.name: Cast acrylic (PMMA) sheet
lines.description: Higher light transmission than polycarbonate at 92 %, and it never yellows. The price is brittleness: fracture toughness is a quarter of polycarbonate, so a hailstone that bounces off PC will punch straight through acrylic.
lines.fabrication: Laser cut cleanly, flame polish edges, solvent cement with dichloromethane. Drill with a modified zero-rake bit or it will crack.
lines.end_of_life: Depolymerises cleanly back to MMA monomer at about 400 °C: one of the very few genuinely closed-loop polymers, and the reason acrylic scores better than its energy figure suggests.

lines.name: PETG sheet
lines.description: The easiest of the clear polymers to thermoform and the only one on this page that is food-contact approved and widely recycled. Poor UV resistance without a coating limits it to indoor and short-term outdoor use.
lines.fabrication: Cold bend, thermoform at 120–140 °C, solvent cement. Needs no drying before forming, unlike polycarbonate.
lines.end_of_life: Recyclable with the PET stream when not co-mingled with PVC; food-contact approved for re-use.

lines.name: UV-stabilised greenhouse polyethylene film
lines.description: By far the cheapest way to enclose a square metre: about $1.75/m² against $28/m² for twin-wall polycarbonate. The catch is a four-year replacement cycle and much poorer insulation, so the life-cycle comparison is far closer than the sticker price suggests.
lines.fabrication: Stretched over hoops and held in extruded aluminium lock channels with a wiggle-wire spring. Double-layer with an inflation blower for a large jump in R-value.
lines.end_of_life: Agricultural film take-back schemes exist in Québec, but a four-year replacement cycle means the cumulative footprint over 20 years is five films, not one.

lines.name: HDPE geomembrane liner, textured
lines.description: Containment liner for lagoons, digester basins and leachate ponds. Chemically inert to the organic acids and ammonia found in manure and silage effluent, which corrode concrete and mild steel.
lines.fabrication: Wedge-welded with a dual-track hot wedge and air-channel tested for leaks; anchored in a perimeter trench.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: EPDM membrane liner
lines.description: Where HDPE geomembrane is stiff and must be welded, EPDM stretches 300 % and conforms to irregular substrates: useful for retrofitting an existing tank or covering a gas holder that changes volume.
lines.fabrication: Seamed with butyl splice tape or contact adhesive; no heat required, which makes field repair simple.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset rubber: crumb-rubber downcycling or energy recovery only.

lines.name: PTFE sheet, virgin
lines.description: Chemically inert to essentially everything, food-contact approved, stable from −200 °C to 260 °C, and the lowest friction of any solid. It also creeps badly under sustained load and cannot be welded or bonded without surface etching.
lines.fabrication: Machined only. Always use a filled grade (glass or bronze) if the part carries sustained compressive load, or it will cold-flow out of the joint.
lines.end_of_life: Not recyclable, and incineration generates persistent fluorinated compounds. Fluoropolymers are under active regulatory pressure: a genuine supply risk for a 20-year design.

lines.name: Nylon 6/6 round bar, extruded
lines.description: The strongest and stiffest of the common machinable polymers, with good fatigue resistance: the standard material for polymer gears and cam followers. Its one serious weakness is moisture: it absorbs up to 2.5 % water, growing dimensionally and losing a third of its stiffness.
lines.fabrication: Machine dry, then condition in water to stabilise dimensions before final inspection. Specify nylon 12 or acetal if dimensional stability in a wet environment is critical.
lines.end_of_life: Depolymerisation routes exist commercially for nylon; dry, clean, single-grade scrap has real value.

lines.name: PVC Schedule 40 socket tee
lines.description: Fittings are where a piping cost estimate is won or lost. A drip system with a lateral every 1.5 m needs hundreds of these, and their combined cost can exceed the pipe itself.
lines.fabrication: Prime and solvent cement. Count every fitting in your bill of materials: students routinely price pipe and forget the fittings.
lines.end_of_life: Recyclable in principle. In practice the chlorine content contaminates mixed-plastic streams and rules out energy recovery without flue-gas scrubbing.

lines.name: HDPE electrofusion coupler
lines.description: Five times the price of the equivalent PVC fitting: and the direct reason HDPE systems cost more to install. What you buy is a joint stronger than the pipe wall, which is why municipal and long-life agricultural mains use it.
lines.fabrication: Scrape the pipe surface to remove the oxidised skin, clamp in an alignment jig, and run the fusion controller. Joint integrity depends entirely on that scraping step.
lines.end_of_life: Mechanically recyclable if clean and separated, but buried pipe is almost never recovered: assume landfill-in-place when you build the life-cycle case.

lines.name: E-glass chopped strand mat, 450 g/m²
lines.description: Randomly oriented short fibres bound with a styrene-soluble binder. Properties are equal in all directions but low: a hand-laid CSM laminate is only about 30 % glass by mass, under 20 % by volume. It is the cheapest way to build thickness and is what most FRP tanks are made of.
lines.fabrication: Hand layup with polyester or vinyl ester resin. Resin uptake is roughly 2.5 times the fabric mass, so budget 1.1 kg of resin per square metre of 450 g mat.
lines.end_of_life: Glass fibre survives the resin but cannot be economically separated from a thermoset matrix; most GFRP is ground and used as filler or landfilled.

lines.name: E-glass woven roving, 600 g/m²
lines.description: Coarse bidirectional weave that builds structural laminate fast. Alternating woven roving with chopped strand mat is the classic tank-and-hull schedule: the mat prevents the roving layers from delaminating.
lines.fabrication: Hand layup or vacuum infusion. Achieves roughly 45 % fibre volume fraction under vacuum, against 30 % by hand.
lines.end_of_life: Glass fibre survives the resin but cannot be economically separated from a thermoset matrix; most GFRP is ground and used as filler or landfilled.

lines.name: E-glass plain-weave cloth, 200 g/m²
lines.description: Fine cloth for surface plies and detail work. Its main structural role is as a barrier ply behind the gelcoat, preventing print-through of the coarse reinforcement underneath.
lines.fabrication: Hand layup. Wet out fully: dry glass in a surface ply wicks water and blisters.
lines.end_of_life: Glass fibre survives the resin but cannot be economically separated from a thermoset matrix; most GFRP is ground and used as filler or landfilled.

lines.name: Flax fibre 2×2 twill, 300 g/m²
lines.description: Québec-grown flax with specific stiffness comparable to E-glass at 57 % the density and a fifth of the embodied energy. It also damps vibration far better than glass. The trade-offs are moisture absorption, batch-to-batch variability and a 180 °C ceiling.
lines.fabrication: Vacuum infusion with a bio-epoxy. Dry the fabric at 80 °C for two hours immediately before layup: absorbed moisture turns to steam and creates voids.
lines.end_of_life: Compostable or energy recovery; the carbon released was absorbed during growth. Note the water figure: natural fibres trade low energy for high agricultural water use.

lines.name: Hemp fibre non-woven mat, 400 g/m²
lines.description: Non-woven hemp from processing residue, the definition of an agricultural waste stream turned into a structural material. Lower properties than woven flax for about two thirds of the price and even lower embodied energy.
lines.fabrication: Compression moulding or infusion. Best suited to semi-structural panels, insulation cores and non-critical enclosures.
lines.end_of_life: Hemp needs no irrigation in most Canadian growing regions, so the water figure is largely green (rainfall) rather than blue (abstracted) water. State which you mean in your report.

lines.name: Jute woven fabric, 350 g/m²
lines.description: The cheapest natural reinforcement and among the lowest embodied energies of any fibre here at about 5.5 MJ/kg. Properties are modest and moisture sensitivity is high, but for a non-structural biocomposite panel core it is hard to beat on a life-cycle basis.
lines.fabrication: Compression mould with a bio-resin. Must be sealed against moisture or the panel swells and delaminates within a season.
lines.end_of_life: The lowest embodied energy of any reinforcement in this catalogue, and fully compostable: but imported, so add transport to your boundary.

lines.name: Carbon fibre 2×2 twill, 200 g/m²
lines.description: Ten times the price of E-glass for about three times the fibre modulus. Include it in your Pugh chart as the high-performance benchmark, then be honest about whether the application can justify the cost and the 280 MJ/kg embodied energy.
lines.fabrication: Vacuum infusion or prepreg autoclave cure. Never bolt carbon directly to aluminium or steel without an insulating layer: the galvanic couple is severe.
lines.end_of_life: Pyrolysis can recover short fibres at roughly 10 % of virgin properties. At 25 kg CO2/kg, carbon fibre must earn its place through mass saving in the use phase.

lines.name: Basalt fibre fabric, 300 g/m²
lines.description: Spun from melted volcanic rock with no additives. Stiffer and far more heat- and alkali-resistant than E-glass, with under half the embodied energy of carbon. A genuinely interesting middle option that most students never consider.
lines.fabrication: Same processing as E-glass. Its alkali resistance makes it the reinforcement of choice for concrete and lime-matrix composites.
lines.end_of_life: Spun from melted basalt rock with no additives or sizing chemistry, which is why its production carbon is half that of E-glass and a twentieth of carbon fibre.

lines.name: General-purpose orthophthalic polyester resin
lines.description: The cheapest laminating resin and the reason FRP is affordable. It shrinks 7–9 % on cure, is attacked by alkalis and hot water, and has poor fatigue resistance: but for a static, ambient-temperature panel it is entirely adequate.
lines.fabrication: Catalyse at 1–2 % MEKP by volume and use within the pot life. Post-cure at 60 °C to reach full properties; an uncured laminate has roughly half its design strength.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset: no recycling route. Styrene emissions during layup are also an occupational-health consideration.

lines.name: Vinyl ester resin, corrosion grade
lines.description: An epoxy backbone with polyester end groups: it processes like polyester but resists acids, alkalis and hot water like an epoxy. This is the standard matrix for chemical tanks and digester internals, at just over double the price of general-purpose polyester.
lines.fabrication: Same catalysis and processing as polyester. Requires a resin-rich corrosion barrier ply at any chemically exposed surface.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset: no recycling route.

lines.name: Laminating epoxy resin system, 2:1
lines.spec: 15 L kit (10 L resin + 5 L hardener)
lines.description: Cures with under 2 % shrinkage and bonds to almost anything, which is why it is the only sensible matrix for natural fibres: polyester shrinkage tears flax and hemp bundles apart during cure.
lines.fabrication: Mix strictly by weight, not volume, and control the exotherm in thick sections. Post-cure to reach the stated glass transition temperature.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset: no recycling route. Its low cure shrinkage is what makes natural-fibre laminates possible, so it is often the enabling choice despite the footprint.

lines.name: Bio-based epoxy, 56 % bio-carbon content
lines.description: Partly derived from plant oils and lignin, cutting embodied energy from about 110 to 52 MJ/kg: a genuine halving. Mechanical properties are roughly 10 % below petroleum epoxy, and the price is 41 % higher, so the case rests on the life-cycle argument.
lines.fabrication: Identical processing to conventional epoxy but with a slightly longer cure. Pair it with flax or hemp for a fully bio-based laminate.
lines.end_of_life: Still a thermoset and still not recyclable, but the bio-carbon content roughly halves the cradle-to-gate energy and carbon against petroleum epoxy.

lines.name: Furan bio-resin, agricultural-residue derived
lines.description: Made from furfuryl alcohol derived from corn cobs and bagasse: a true agricultural-waste-derived thermoset. It is stiffer and far more fire- and chemical-resistant than epoxy, and also more brittle. Its natural char formation is a real asset in a fire-code argument.
lines.fabrication: Acid catalysed with a controlled exotherm. It cures dark brown and releases water during cure, so the layup must be vented.
lines.end_of_life: Derived from corn cobs and bagasse: a genuine agricultural-residue thermoset. Chars rather than melts in fire, which also helps the fire-code argument.

lines.name: FRP flat panel, isophthalic polyester/CSM
lines.description: Ready-made glass-reinforced panel: no layup required. Completely immune to the fertiliser salts and manure acids that destroy galvanised steel, and electrically non-conductive, which matters near electrical service.
lines.fabrication: Cut with a diamond or carbide blade under dust extraction. Seal every cut edge with resin: an unsealed edge wicks water into the laminate.
lines.end_of_life: Ground as filler or landfilled. Its case rests on outlasting the galvanised steel it replaces by two to three times.

lines.name: Moulded FRP grating, vinyl ester
lines.description: Walkway and platform grating for chemically aggressive areas: digester decks, fertiliser plants, wash-down floors. Roughly triple the price of galvanised steel bar grating, and it will still be there when the steel has rusted through twice.
lines.fabrication: Cut with a diamond blade and coat cut ends with vinyl ester. Support spacing governs deflection: FRP is far less stiff than steel and deflects visibly.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset pultrusion: cement-kiln co-processing is the only established route, recovering the energy and the glass as clinker feed.

lines.name: Pultruded FRP square tube, vinyl ester
lines.description: Set this against the galvanised HSS and the aluminium tube of the same nominal size. It will never corrode and is non-conductive, but it is not light: at 1.90 kg/m it is heavier than the 6061 tube, and with a modulus of 17 GPa against 200 for steel the frame will be deflection-governed, not strength-governed.
lines.fabrication: Cut with a diamond blade; join with bonded or bolted brackets. Pultrusions are strongly anisotropic: nearly all fibres run lengthwise, so transverse and bearing strength are low.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset pultrusion: cement-kiln co-processing is the only established route, recovering the energy and the glass as clinker feed.

lines.name: Pultruded FRP wide-flange beam
lines.description: Structural section for corrosive-environment framing. Design it to a deflection limit rather than a stress limit and check the flanges for local buckling: FRP sections buckle long before they yield.
lines.fabrication: Bolted connections with oversized washers to spread bearing load; never weld or hot-form.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset pultrusion: cement-kiln co-processing is the only established route, recovering the energy and the glass as clinker feed.

lines.name: Isophthalic NPG gelcoat, white
lines.description: The pigmented surface layer that gives an FRP part its weather resistance and finish. Without it the laminate's surface glass fibres wick moisture and the part blisters: the failure mode behind most cheap fibreglass tanks.
lines.fabrication: Sprayed or brushed into the mould at 0.5–0.6 mm and allowed to gel before the first laminate ply goes on. Too thick and it cracks; too thin and it never fully cures.
lines.end_of_life: Thermoset surface layer; no recycling route, but it is what prevents blistering and doubles the panel's service life.

lines.name: Cross-linked PVC structural foam core
lines.description: A sandwich core does for a panel exactly what the web does for an I-beam: separating two thin skins by 15 mm raises bending stiffness by roughly two orders of magnitude for almost no mass. It also happens to insulate at 0.031 W/m·K.
lines.fabrication: Vacuum bagged between skins; score or perforate the core so resin can flow and lock the skins together.
lines.end_of_life: Cross-linked PVC foam: not re-meltable. Offcuts are typically landfilled, and core waste on a curved part can exceed 30 %.

lines.name: End-grain balsa core
lines.description: End-grain balsa carries roughly eight times the compressive stress of PVC foam at twice the density, and its embodied energy is 4 MJ/kg against 100 for the foam. Its weakness is rot if water ever reaches it: every fastener penetration must be sealed.
lines.fabrication: Vacuum bagged with an epoxy or vinyl ester. Bore out and fill every through-fastener location with thickened resin before drilling.
lines.end_of_life: Carbon-negative while the stored biogenic carbon remains locked in the panel. Rots if water reaches it, so the seal detail decides whether that carbon stays stored.

lines.name: Wheat-straw particle board, formaldehyde-free
lines.description: Made from wheat straw that would otherwise be burnt or ploughed under, bonded with a formaldehyde-free MDI resin. It performs like a good particle board, stores biogenic carbon, and is directly relevant to any agricultural-waste panel brief.
lines.fabrication: Cut and machine like wood. Must be edge-sealed and kept out of standing water; it is not a structural sheathing on its own.
lines.end_of_life: Diverts wheat straw from field burning and stores its carbon for the building's life. Formaldehyde-free MDI binder also keeps indoor air quality within code.

lines.name: Hemp-lime (hempcrete) block
lines.description: Hemp shiv bound in a lime matrix. It is not structural: it infills a timber or steel frame: but it is carbon-negative over its life, regulates humidity passively, and is non-combustible. Embodied energy of 2.5 MJ/kg is the lowest in this catalogue.
lines.fabrication: Laid in a lime mortar or cast in situ around a frame. Needs a breathable lime render, never a cement one, or trapped moisture will rot the frame.
lines.end_of_life: The lowest embodied energy in this catalogue. The lime matrix continues to carbonate and absorb CO2 for decades after installation; it can be crushed and returned to soil.

lines.name: Flax/bio-epoxy structural insulated panel
lines.description: A complete bio-composite building panel: flax/bio-epoxy skins over a bio-foam core, R-value around 3.5 per 25 mm. This is the closest product in the catalogue to what a sustainable-construction brief actually asks you to design.
lines.fabrication: Panels are splined and bonded at joints. Fire performance must be verified against the building code: bio-resins char rather than melt, which helps, but a tested assembly rating is still required.
lines.end_of_life: Bio-skins and bio-core; separable at end of life only if mechanically fastened rather than bonded.

lines.name: AISI M2 high-speed steel flat ground stock
lines.description: Tungsten-molybdenum high-speed steel keeps its 64 HRC hardness to about 600 °C: that red hardness is the whole point, and it is why sawmill and planer knives are made from it rather than plain carbon steel.
lines.fabrication: Grind to shape in the hardened condition with copious coolant; burning the edge draws the temper locally and it will fail there first.
lines.end_of_life: Tungsten and molybdenum make this the highest-carbon tool steel here, but HSS scrap is separately collected because those elements are valuable.

lines.name: AISI D2 cold-work tool steel plate
lines.description: Twelve percent chromium gives a huge volume of hard carbides: outstanding abrasion resistance and near-zero size change through heat treatment. That carbide volume also makes it brittle, so keep it away from impact.
lines.fabrication: Rough machine annealed, air harden (which is why it is dimensionally stable), then finish grind. Wire EDM is common for die profiles.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as high-chromium alloy scrap.

lines.name: AISI A2 air-hardening tool steel plate
lines.description: The sensible middle of the tool-steel range: most of D2's wear resistance with noticeably better toughness. When a student's Pugh chart is deadlocked between D2 and S7, A2 is usually the honest answer.
lines.fabrication: Air hardens with minimal distortion, so it can be finish machined close to size before heat treatment.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as alloy tool-steel scrap.

lines.name: AISI O1 oil-hardening flat ground stock
lines.description: The cheapest genuine tool steel and the easiest to heat treat in a small shop: it hardens from a simple oil quench at 800 °C. Excellent for knife edges and low-volume cutting tools where hot hardness is not required.
lines.fabrication: Harden in oil and temper immediately; O1 will crack if left untempered overnight. Expect about 0.1 % size change on quench.
lines.end_of_life: The least alloyed tool steel here, and correspondingly the easiest to recycle and the lowest in carbon.

lines.name: AISI S7 shock-resisting tool steel plate
lines.description: Deliberately traded hardness for toughness: fracture toughness near 45 MPa·m^0.5 against 16 for D2, at the cost of four points of hardness. This is the material for chipper anvils, shear blades and anything that takes a hammering.
lines.fabrication: Air hardens; can be finish machined before treatment. Do not push hardness above 58 HRC or you lose the toughness you bought it for.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as alloy scrap. Its toughness means parts are re-ground rather than scrapped, extending life several times over.

lines.name: AISI H13 hot-work tool steel plate
lines.description: Designed to resist thermal fatigue: the network of heat-checking cracks that destroys dies cycling between hot and cold. For a pellet-mill die running at 90 °C under continuous compression, this resistance matters more than raw hardness.
lines.fabrication: Machine annealed, vacuum harden and double temper. Nitride the working surface (MFW-HT-NITRIDE) for wear resistance without losing core toughness.
lines.end_of_life: Recycled as hot-work alloy scrap; dies are typically re-nitrided and returned to service two or three times first.

lines.name: WC-10Co cemented carbide blank, ground
lines.description: Tungsten carbide grains in a cobalt binder: about three times the stiffness of steel and ten times the abrasive wear life, with essentially zero ductility. The 10 % cobalt grade trades a little hardness for enough toughness to survive intermittent cutting.
lines.fabrication: Cannot be machined conventionally. Shape by diamond grinding, wire EDM or as-sintered near-net form; braze or clamp it onto a steel body.
lines.end_of_life: Carbide scrap is worth more per kilogramme than most finished steels, and zinc-reclaim recycling recovers over 95 % of it. High production carbon, but an unusually closed loop.

lines.name: WC-6Co brazable tip insert
lines.description: The tip that gets brazed onto a steel blade body: the standard construction for carbide-tipped saw and plough blades. You buy carbide only where the wear happens and keep tough, cheap steel everywhere else. That is materials selection in one product.
lines.fabrication: Silver-brazed to a steel body with a stress-relieving shim to accommodate the better than two-fold mismatch in thermal expansion, then diamond ground.
lines.end_of_life: Carbide scrap is worth more per kilogramme than most finished steels, and zinc-reclaim recycling recovers over 95 % of it. High production carbon, but an unusually closed loop.

lines.name: WC-10Co solid carbide rod, ground
lines.description: Solid rod for end mills and wear pins. At $742 per metre it is the most expensive stock item in this catalogue: a useful reminder that carbide is bought by the cubic centimetre, not the kilogram.
lines.fabrication: Diamond ground or EDM only. Handle carefully; it chips if dropped on a hard floor.
lines.end_of_life: Carbide scrap is worth more per kilogramme than most finished steels, and zinc-reclaim recycling recovers over 95 % of it. High production carbon, but an unusually closed loop.

lines.name: Stellite 6 cobalt hardfacing rod
lines.description: A cobalt-chromium-tungsten alloy that keeps its hardness to 800 °C and resists corrosion at the same time: the combination is rare and expensive. Used to hard-face valve seats and food-processing knives where a steel weld overlay would corrode.
lines.fabrication: Deposited by GTAW or PTA over a buttered stainless layer; the substrate must be preheated to avoid cracking the deposit.
lines.end_of_life: Cobalt is a critical raw material with significant mining impacts; worn hardfacing is recovered where the deposit is thick enough to strip.

lines.name: Tungsten carbide composite hardfacing rod
lines.description: Crushed carbide granules in a nickel or iron matrix, deposited by torch or arc. The go-to repair for worn plough shares, auger flights and mixer paddles: often more economical than replacing the part, which is a legitimate line in a life-cycle cost analysis.
lines.fabrication: Applied by oxy-acetylene or GMAW in a stringer pattern. Not machinable afterwards; it must be ground.
lines.end_of_life: Rebuilding a worn part with hardfacing avoids manufacturing a replacement entirely: often the lowest-carbon option available, even though the rod itself is carbon-intensive.

lines.name: 99.5 % alumina ceramic plate
lines.description: Harder than any steel, chemically inert, an electrical insulator, and usable to 1700 °C. It is also brittle, with a fracture toughness of 4 MPa·m^0.5, about a thirtieth of mild steel, so it must never see tensile or bending stress.
lines.fabrication: Supplied as-fired or ground. Bond into a compliant mount with a resilient adhesive; a rigid clamp will crack it on the first thermal cycle.
lines.end_of_life: Chemically inert and safe to landfill; can be crushed as refractory aggregate.

lines.name: Sintered silicon carbide wear tile
lines.description: Harder than alumina with four times the thermal conductivity, so it survives thermal shock far better. Tiles like these are epoxy-bonded into a mosaic to line chutes and cyclones handling abrasive biomass.
lines.fabrication: Bonded into a steel backing with a flexible epoxy that lets adjacent tiles move independently. Individual tiles are replaceable: an important maintainability argument.
lines.end_of_life: Individual tiles are replaceable, so the mosaic is repaired rather than replaced: a maintainability argument with a real carbon dividend.

lines.name: Yttria-stabilised zirconia (Y-TZP) rod
lines.description: Transformation toughening gives zirconia a fracture toughness of about 10 MPa·m^0.5: two and a half times alumina, and the reason it is the only ceramic used for knife blades. Its very low thermal conductivity also makes it a thermal barrier.
lines.fabrication: Diamond ground. Avoid prolonged exposure to 200–300 °C in humid air, which causes low-temperature degradation and surface spalling.
lines.end_of_life: Zirconium is energy-intensive to refine; inert at end of life.

lines.name: Silicon nitride bearing ball, Grade 5
lines.description: Hybrid bearings with ceramic balls in steel races run faster and cooler, need no lubricant, and are immune to the corrosion that kills steel bearings in wash-down and slurry service. At 40 % the density of steel, centrifugal loading drops sharply too.
lines.fabrication: Supplied finish-lapped. Handle with clean gloves: surface contamination initiates spalling.
lines.end_of_life: High production carbon, but ceramic hybrid bearings run unlubricated and last several times longer than steel, moving the balance in the use phase.

lines.name: TiN PVD coating service
lines.spec: Per m² of coated surface ($34.00 per dm²), 5 dm² minimum
lines.description: A 2–4 µm titanium nitride layer at 2300 HV: the familiar gold coating on drill bits. It roughly triples tool life for a few dollars per part and is food-contact approved, unlike most hard coatings.
lines.fabrication: Deposited at 450 °C, so the substrate must already be hardened and tempered above that temperature or it will soften in the chamber. Surfaces must be polished before coating: PVD replicates every scratch.
lines.process_note: Per dm². Vacuum PVD on the Québec grid; the coating triples tool life, so it usually pays back many times in avoided tool manufacture.

lines.name: WC-Co HVOF thermal spray coating
lines.spec: Per m² of coated surface ($92.00 per dm²), 5 dm² minimum
lines.description: High-velocity oxy-fuel spraying puts a 100–300 µm carbide layer onto a steel part: thick enough to rebuild worn dimensions, unlike PVD. It is the standard repair for pellet-mill rollers and pump sleeves.
lines.fabrication: Grit blast, spray, then diamond grind to final size. The bond is mechanical, so surface preparation determines whether the coating stays on.
lines.process_note: Per dm². Oxy-fuel combustion plus carbide powder, roughly half of which overspray is lost.

lines.name: Diamond-like carbon (DLC) coating
lines.spec: Per m² of coated surface ($58.00 per dm²), 5 dm² minimum
lines.description: Hardest of the commercial coatings at up to 3000 HV with a friction coefficient near 0.1: it is effectively a solid lubricant. Its 350 °C ceiling rules out hot-work applications.
lines.fabrication: Low-temperature PVD, so it will not temper a hardened substrate. Requires a very smooth, clean base surface.
lines.process_note: Per dm². Low-temperature PVD, low direct carbon.

lines.name: Hard chrome electroplating
lines.spec: Per m² of coated surface ($26.00 per dm²), 10 dm² minimum
lines.description: The cheapest hard surface per square decimetre and the traditional choice for hydraulic rods. It is also the environmental problem child of this page: hexavalent chromium plating faces tightening regulation, which is a real supply-chain risk for a 20-year design.
lines.fabrication: Plated 20–50 µm and ground to size. The coating is micro-cracked by design, so a nickel underlayer is required for genuine corrosion protection.
lines.process_note: Per dm². Hexavalent chromium plating carries significant effluent treatment and a tightening regulatory outlook.

lines.name: Bi-metal M42/carbon steel bandsaw blade stock
lines.description: An electron-beam welded strip of M42 high-speed steel on a spring-steel back: hard teeth on a flexible body. It is the clearest everyday example of using two materials where one cannot do both jobs, and it is central to the sawmill-blade brief.
lines.fabrication: Supplied in coil and welded into a loop by the saw shop. Tooth pitch selection matters as much as the material: too fine and the gullet packs with sawdust and the blade overheats.
lines.end_of_life: Two welded steels: recycles as mixed alloy scrap. Using expensive HSS only at the teeth is itself a material-efficiency strategy.

lines.name: 3-axis CNC milling
lines.description: The default cost basis for a machined prismatic part. When you compare aluminium against steel, remember that aluminium cuts three to four times faster: often reversing the material-price ranking at the finished-part level.
lines.fabrication: Includes programming for simple parts. Complex 3D surfacing is quoted separately.
lines.process_note: Electric load on the Québec grid, which emits about 1.5 g CO2/kWh. The identical job in Alberta would emit roughly 7.5 kg CO2 per hour: a 300-fold difference from location alone.

lines.name: 5-axis CNC milling
lines.description: Needed for impellers, turbine blade roots and any part with compound-angle features. At more than twice the 3-axis rate, a design change that keeps the part 3-axis machinable is often worth more than any material substitution.
lines.fabrication: Quote requires a 3D model. Fixture design is charged separately for first articles.
lines.process_note: Higher spindle and axis load. Grid carbon as above.

lines.name: CNC turning
lines.description: For shafts, rollers, bushings and anything with an axis of revolution. Bar-fed production drops the effective rate sharply above about 50 pieces.
lines.fabrication: Includes standard tolerance of ±0.05 mm. Tighter tolerances need a grinding operation.
lines.process_note: Electric load; chips are collected and returned to the melt.

lines.name: Manual mill / lathe / fitting
lines.description: The cheapest route for a single prototype piece, because there is no programming or setup overhead to amortise. Above roughly five pieces CNC becomes cheaper: the classic break-even calculation.
lines.fabrication: Best for jigs, fixtures, modifications and repair work.
lines.process_note: Lowest process energy of any machining route: a reminder that for one prototype, the simplest process is usually also the lightest.

lines.name: Fibre laser cutting, 6 kW
lines.spec: Shop rate; steel to 20 mm, stainless to 15 mm
lines.description: Fast, narrow kerf, near-zero taper and a very small heat-affected zone. A fibre source cuts aluminium and copper to moderate thickness, with more dross than on steel; it cannot cut any non-metal.
lines.fabrication: Nesting efficiency drives the price: parts nested tightly on a full sheet cost far less per piece than the same parts cut individually.
lines.process_note: Includes nitrogen or oxygen assist gas. Tight nesting reduces both cost and material carbon.

lines.name: Abrasive waterjet cutting
lines.spec: Shop rate; any material to 150 mm
lines.description: The only process here that cuts anything: hardened tool steel, titanium, glass, stone, FRP and composite laminate: with no heat-affected zone at all. It is slow, which is why it is the most expensive hourly rate on the cutting page.
lines.fabrication: Essential for AR500 and tool steel, where flame cutting would ruin the temper, and for composite panels, where a saw blade delaminates the edge.
lines.process_note: Garnet abrasive dominates the footprint: roughly 25 kg per hour, mined, shipped and then landfilled as slurry.

lines.name: CNC plasma cutting
lines.spec: Per metre of cut, steel to 25 mm
lines.description: The cheapest way to cut thick mild steel by a wide margin. Kerf is wide and tapered and the heat-affected zone extends a millimetre or two, so allow machining stock on any surface that matters.
lines.fabrication: Not suitable for stainless in food service without removing the oxidised cut edge: the HAZ is chromium depleted and will corrode.
lines.process_note: Per metre of cut. Wide kerf means more material converted to dross than with laser.

lines.name: GMAW (MIG) welding
lines.description: The productivity workhorse for structural steel: high deposition rate, easily automated, and forgiving. Not suitable for out-of-position work on thin sheet or for sanitary joints.
lines.fabrication: Weld cost estimates should be built from deposited weld metal volume, not guesswork. A 6 mm fillet costs roughly four times a 3 mm fillet per metre.
lines.process_note: Shielding gas dominates: argon–CO2 mixtures are released directly to atmosphere at 15–20 L/min.

lines.name: GTAW (TIG) welding
lines.description: Slow, clean and fully controllable: the only manual process acceptable for thin stainless, aluminium and any joint that must be crevice-free after grinding. Expect roughly a third the deposition rate of GMAW.
lines.fabrication: Requires argon back-purge on stainless and titanium. Budget for the purge gas and dam materials, not just the arc time.
lines.process_note: Pure argon shielding at a lower flow rate; slower deposition but a much smaller gas burden per hour.

lines.name: SMAW (stick) welding
lines.description: The field process: no shielding gas to blow away, works on rusty and painted material, and needs only a power source. Deposition rate and quality are the lowest of the three, and slag must be chipped between passes.
lines.fabrication: The realistic choice for on-farm repair, which is a legitimate maintainability argument in an agricultural design.
lines.process_note: No shielding gas at all: the flux does the work. Often the lowest-carbon welding process available in the field.

lines.name: Orbital tube welding, sanitary certified
lines.description: Automated, fully documented, repeatable full-penetration tube welds with a smooth internal profile. Required for 3-A compliance in a milk line: a hand-made joint cannot meet the internal surface specification.
lines.fabrication: Requires square-cut, deburred tube ends, full argon purge and a weld coupon record for every joint. That documentation is much of what you are paying for.
lines.process_note: Per weld, including the internal argon purge that sanitary work requires.

lines.name: Quench and temper
lines.spec: Per kg of load, 25 kg minimum
lines.description: Turns an ordinary carbon or alloy steel into a high-strength one. On a $7.40/kg basis this is often cheaper than upgrading the alloy, which is exactly the sort of comparison a Pugh chart should surface.
lines.fabrication: Specify the target hardness range, not the process. Distortion is unavoidable: leave grinding stock on critical surfaces.
lines.process_note: Per kg of load, gas-fired furnace. Heat treating a cheap steel is often lower-carbon than specifying a more heavily alloyed one.
