lines.name: Carburising / case hardening
lines.spec: Per kg of load, 25 kg minimum
lines.description: Diffuses carbon into the surface to give a 0.5–1.5 mm case at 60 HRC over a tough, ductile core. It is how gear teeth and cam lobes get a hard wear surface without becoming brittle throughout.
lines.fabrication: Mask any surface that must stay soft, or machine the case off afterwards. Case depth must be specified: it drives cost more than part mass.
lines.process_note: Per kg. Long furnace cycles at 900 °C make carburising the most energy-intensive heat treatment here.

lines.name: Gas nitriding
lines.spec: Per kg of load, 25 kg minimum
lines.description: Runs at 500–530 °C, below the tempering temperature, so the part barely moves: the deciding advantage for a finish-machined die or a long slender shaft. Case is thin (0.2–0.5 mm) but reaches 1000 HV.
lines.fabrication: Only works on nitriding steels containing aluminium, chromium or molybdenum: 4140 and H13 nitride well, plain 1018 does not.
lines.process_note: Per kg. Long cycle at lower temperature, plus ammonia dissociation.

lines.name: Stress-relief anneal
lines.spec: Per kg of load, 25 kg minimum
lines.description: Relieves the residual stress left by welding, machining and forming. Skip it on a welded frame and the part will move during final machining or in its first thermal cycle in service.
lines.fabrication: Specify for any welded assembly that will be finish machined, and for any part that must hold tolerance over a long service life.
lines.process_note: Per kg. Cheap in both money and carbon, and it prevents the distortion that would otherwise scrap the part.

lines.name: Hot-dip galvanising to ASTM A123
lines.spec: Per kg of load, 50 kg minimum
lines.description: The cheapest durable corrosion protection there is. An 85 µm coating on a rural structure gives 50 years or more to first maintenance, which is why it is the default for agricultural steelwork.
lines.fabrication: Assemblies must have vent and drain holes at every enclosed section, or the trapped air will explode in the 450 °C kettle. Design those holes in from the start.
lines.process_note: Per kg, including the zinc coating itself. Adds about 10 % to the steel's cradle-to-gate carbon and removes decades of repainting from the use phase.

lines.name: Polyester powder coating
lines.description: A tough, colour-fast, solvent-free finish. On its own it is a barrier coating only: one scratch through to the steel and undercutting rust begins, which is why the best specification is galvanise first, then powder coat over it.
lines.fabrication: Requires blast cleaning and phosphate pretreatment. Cures at 200 °C, so it cannot be applied over most polymers or heat-sensitive assemblies.
lines.process_note: Per m². Solvent-free, but the 200 °C cure oven dominates the energy.

lines.name: Fusion-bonded epoxy coating
lines.description: The pipeline coating: thick, chemically resistant, and formulated for buried and immersed service where powder coat would fail. Standard for buried tanks and epoxy-coated steel digesters.
lines.fabrication: Applied to a preheated blast-cleaned surface. Field joints and damage must be patched with a compatible liquid epoxy or the holiday becomes a corrosion cell.
lines.process_note: Per m². Preheat plus cure; formulated for buried service where a thinner coating would fail early.

lines.name: Citric acid passivation to ASTM A967
lines.description: Dissolves free iron left on a stainless surface by cutting, forming and grinding, then lets the chromium oxide film reform fully. Skip it and a perfectly specified 316L part will show rust spots within weeks: a very common and entirely avoidable failure.
lines.fabrication: Citric acid has largely replaced nitric acid: it works as well, is not an oxidiser, and the spent bath is far easier to treat.
lines.process_note: Per kg. Citric acid has displaced nitric: comparable performance, far lower effluent treatment burden.

lines.name: Electropolishing
lines.spec: Per m² of surface ($1.95 per dm²), 5 dm² minimum
lines.description: Removes 10–40 µm of the deformed surface layer electrochemically, typically halving Ra and enriching the surface in chromium. It is the standard finish for aseptic process equipment.
lines.fabrication: Weld beads must be ground flush first; electropolishing exaggerates any surface defect rather than hiding it.
lines.process_note: Per dm². The spent electrolyte is metal-bearing hazardous waste: the highest-impact step in a sanitary fabrication.

lines.name: Press-brake forming
lines.spec: Per bend, up to 3 m length
lines.description: Each bend is a discrete cost, so a part with twelve bends costs $102 in forming before any material. Redesigning to eight bends is usually a bigger saving than any material substitution.
lines.fabrication: Minimum inside bend radius is roughly one material thickness for mild steel and three for 6061-T6 aluminium; too tight and the outer fibre cracks.
lines.process_note: Per bend. Negligible energy; the carbon question with forming is how much material the blank wastes.

lines.name: Injection mould tooling, aluminium prototype
lines.description: A non-recurring engineering charge that must be divided across your production volume. Over 500 parts it adds $13.60 each; over 50,000 parts it adds $0.14. Getting this amortisation right is the whole point of a production-volume analysis.
lines.fabrication: Aluminium tooling is good for roughly 10,000 shots. Hardened steel tooling costs three to four times more and lasts a million.
lines.process_note: One-off tooling. Amortise this over your production volume before comparing it with anything.

lines.name: Injection moulding, per part
lines.description: Once the tool exists, each part costs little more than its material and a few seconds of machine time. This is why a moulded polymer component beats a machined one above a few thousand pieces and loses badly below a few hundred.
lines.fabrication: Includes material for a part of roughly 50 g. Cycle time, not material, dominates the per-part cost on thick sections.
lines.process_note: Per part, excluding the polymer itself. Cycle energy is small; the material choice dominates.

lines.name: Rotational moulding setup
lines.description: The economical route to large hollow polyethylene parts: spray tanks, hopper liners, digester vessels. Tooling is a fraction of injection-mould cost because there is no injection pressure to contain.
lines.fabrication: Wall thickness is set by charge mass and is inherently variable; do not design a rotomoulded part with tight wall tolerance.
lines.process_note: One-off tooling for large hollow parts.

lines.name: Aluminium extrusion die
lines.description: A custom extrusion profile lets you integrate glazing channel, drainage gutter and fastener slot into a single part, deleting several assembly operations. Worth it above roughly 300 m of production.
lines.fabrication: Symmetric profiles with uniform wall thickness extrude cleanly; thin fins and sharp internal corners drive up die cost and scrap.
lines.process_note: One-off die. A profile that deletes assembly operations can repay its die carbon quickly.

lines.name: Vacuum infusion layup labour
lines.description: Skilled labour is the dominant cost in any composite part: usually well over half. This is the single largest reason natural-fibre composites struggle to compete with stamped steel on a finished-part basis.
lines.fabrication: Includes consumables (bagging film, peel ply, flow media, tubing), which typically add 15–20 % to material cost on every part.
lines.process_note: Per hour, dominated by single-use consumables: bagging film, peel ply, flow media and tubing, all landfilled after one cure.

lines.name: Mill test report / CMTR retrieval
lines.description: Material traceability documentation. Any food-contact, pressure-containing or code-governed component needs it, and unheard-of as it may seem, the paperwork is sometimes the difference between an acceptable and a rejected installation.
lines.fabrication: Order it with the material: retrieving a certificate after the fact is often impossible once the heat is consumed.
lines.process_note: Documentation only.

lines.name: Dye penetrant inspection
lines.description: Reveals surface-breaking cracks in welds and castings on any non-porous material. It is the cheapest weld inspection there is and finds the defects that matter most in fatigue-loaded parts.
lines.fabrication: Surface must be clean and free of paint. It finds only surface defects: subsurface porosity needs radiography or ultrasonics.
lines.process_note: Per part, including solvent penetrant and developer.

lines.name: Ultrasonic weld inspection
lines.description: Detects internal lack of fusion and porosity in full-penetration welds. Required by code on pressure-containing welds: a digester tank shell, for example: and a legitimate line item in any safety-critical cost estimate.
lines.fabrication: Requires a smooth scanning surface and a calibration block of the same material and thickness.
lines.process_note: Per hour. Couplant and electrical load only.

briefs.title: Agricultural Tractor Plough Blade
briefs.candidate_families: High-carbon steel vs. alloy steel vs. carbide-tipped steel
briefs.context: A mouldboard plough for a 120 hp tractor working stony clay loam in the Montérégie. The share is the wearing edge: it cuts the furrow, carries the soil load onto the mouldboard, and hits the occasional rock at field speed. Shares are consumables and the farm replaces a set every season or two.

requirements.text: Resist abrasive wear from soil and grit over a full season
Survive rock impacts at working speed without fracturing
Hold a cutting edge, or be sharpenable in the farm workshop
Be replaceable by the farmer with hand tools
Keep the cost per hectare worked below the cost of the fuel a sharp edge saves

constraints: Batch of 200 shares a year for the dealer network
Must be weldable or brazeable for hardfacing or tip repair
No coating that cannot survive soil abrasion
briefs.deliverable: A justified selection: the candidates you weighed, the weighting you argued from and why, the scored matrix, and a quotation for the line you chose at the quantity the project needs. The report is marked on the justification, not on the pick.

briefs.title: Biomass Pellet Mill Die Components
briefs.candidate_families: Tool steel vs. tungsten carbide vs. ceramic-coated steel
briefs.context: A ring die and roller shells for a 5 t/h biomass pellet mill compressing wood and straw at 90 to 110 °C. The die's channels see sliding abrasion from silica in the feed and cyclic pressure every revolution; a die is scrapped when the channels wear open and pellet density falls.

requirements.text: Resist abrasive wear in the die channels
Keep channel dimensions stable through thermal cycling
Survive cyclic compressive loading without fatigue cracking
Be machinable or formable into a drilled ring with thousands of channels
Be re-manufacturable or re-coatable at end of life

constraints: Replacement every 2 000 h is a known operating cost; a longer life must earn it
Food contact is not required, but no heavy-metal coating that could reach the feed
One die per mill, four mills on the site

Resist wind uplift and racking
Survive the humid interior without corrosion for the design life
Limit thermal expansion so glazing seals stay tight
Be assembled on site by a small crew with bolted connections

briefs.context: The knives of a 150 mm disc chipper fed with green hardwood and the odd nail or stone from the landing. Each knife is struck thousands of times an hour and is removed, ground and refitted on a schedule.

Hold an edge between regrinds
Survive a stray nail or stone with a dent rather than a fracture
Be resharpened on a surface grinder in the shop

Survive summer sun on the surface laterals
Resist fertigation chemicals and chlorinated water
Survive soil loading, frost heave and ground movement when buried
Be joined in the field with hand tools or with tooling the farm can rent
